q1.where: Sheet 1, key message box (cleft on the left side)

q2.answer: In the bone of the gum, next to the front teeth, where the upper jaw bone has a gap. It is called the alveolar cleft.
q2.where: Sheet 1, 'What this model shows' and key message box

q3.answer: The small tooth next to the front tooth (the lateral incisor) on the left side never grew. About half of children with a cleft do not have this tooth on the cleft side.

q4.answer: The eye tooth needs bone to grow down into. The graft gives it bone to come down into.
q4.where: Sheet 1, 'The eye tooth' and 'Why surgeons do the bone graft'

q5.answer: Most teams do it at about 8 to 11 years old, chosen by how far the teeth have grown rather than by age, ideally before the eye tooth comes through the gum.

q6.answer: Most often from the hip (soft, spongy bone).

q7.answer: New bone fills the gap and the gum has healed over it. The eye tooth is still in the bone but a little lower than before.
q7.where: Sheet 2, key message box and 'What has changed'

q8.answer: With an X-ray at about 3 to 6 months after surgery, which shows how well the new bone has taken.

q9.answer: Your hip can be sore for a while after the bone is taken. In one study children went back to school about 2 weeks after surgery.

q10.answer: It has come down through the new bone (the graft) and is fully in the row of teeth. Some get stuck and need a small operation to uncover them.
q10.where: Sheet 3, 'What has changed' and key message box

q11.answer: Fixed braces line up the teeth. Almost everyone who has this graft needs them.

q12.answer: Two main plans. Close the space: braces move the eye tooth into the missing tooth's place and the dentist reshapes it, which is most often used for children with a cleft. Keep the space: a removable plate with a false tooth while growing, then when growth stops an implant (post with a crown) or a bridge (false tooth with one wing glued behind the next tooth). The cleft team will talk with you about which suits you.
